object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: An occurrence of a failure or problem in a service that requires investigation and resolution. Created when a problem is detected through monitoring, customer report, or engineer observation.

source_references.excerpt: Okay. Something breaks. We find out about it, one way or another. Somebody declares an incident... Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an incident, in the format INC- followed by a sequence number.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence... Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: Classification of technical impact and blast radius of an incident. SEV1 is everything down for everyone; SEV4 is degraded or cosmetic.

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact. SEV1 is everything's down for everyone. SEV4 is degraded, cosmetic, one region, nobody's really suffering.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: Classification of urgency based on customer impact and commercial consequences. P1 is highest priority; P4 is lowest.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4... Priority is about customer urgency. Who's affected, what they've promised their own customers, whether we're breaching an SLA.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: Current state of an incident. Triage (under investigation), declared (confirmed and assigned), mitigated (temporary fix), resolved (permanent fix), or closed (closed out).

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed... Exactly one at a time.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A signal from the monitoring platform indicating a potential problem. Can be automatically generated or manually created by an engineer.

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert... If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an alert, generated by the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: And an alert -- identified how? Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: CustomerTicket
object_types.definition: A support ticket created when a customer reports a problem. Tickets can result in the creation of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: the alert fires and support gets three tickets in the same two minutes... You have to raise a ticket first and link it.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for a customer support ticket, from a different system than incidents.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A system, platform, or component that can be affected by an incident and is owned by a team.

source_references.excerpt: And an incident affects a service?... Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.name: ServiceName
object_types.definition: Unique name of a service, enforced in the service catalogue.

source_references.excerpt: Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: A group that owns and is responsible for one or more services.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority appear to be independent (lines 63-79 explicitly establish non-correlation), but this was stated as an observation about how they currently work, not necessarily a formal constraint. Should the model enforce that a P1 is NOT always a SEV1, or is this just a descriptive finding?

source_references.excerpt: Are they correlated at all?... A P1 is always a SEV1... That is not true... It's not true in practice either, and it's the assumption that gets us in trouble.

ambiguities.description: Incident state transitions are not explicitly modeled. The five states exist but the valid transitions between them are not defined. Can an incident transition directly from triage to resolved, or only through declared and mitigated first?

source_references.excerpt: What are the states?... Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority can change during the incident (lines 91-97 discuss severity changes in the timeline), but the current model only captures their current values. Should historical versions or the entire timeline be modeled, or is current-state sufficient?

source_references.excerpt: Can either change during the incident?... Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: Duplicates cardinality interpretation: The model captures that an incident can be a duplicate of at most one other incident. However, the inverse cardinality (how many incidents can duplicate the same primary) is not explicitly constrained. Can an incident be the primary for many duplicates?

source_references.excerpt: You link them. One is the primary and the others get marked as duplicates of it... Incident B is a duplicate of incident A.

ambiguities.description: Customer-caused incidents classification: Lines 217-253 discuss whether incidents found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified or excluded from reliability metrics. The decision is explicitly parked and not captured in the current model. Should a cause_classification or incident_type attribute be added once a decision is made?

source_references.excerpt: Support raises tickets. Some of those tickets become incidents... A meaningful number of those turn out to be user error... the incident record carries the current severity... The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: Mandatory commander constraint in context of incident state: The rule states 'Declared incidents have exactly one commander; Triage incidents have none.' This is conditional on state, not universal. The current model has a conditional mandatory constraint, but this requires special handling: a commander is optional for triage incidents but mandatory for declared incidents. Is this captured correctly as a single constraint, or should it be split into two state-specific constraints?

source_references.excerpt: An incident starts in triage. In triage there's no commander, that's the point of triage: someone's looking at whether this is even real. A commander is assigned when it's declared... Declared incidents have exactly one commander. Triage incidents have none.

ambiguities.description: Incident affects Service cardinality: The model states 'An incident affects one or more services.' This is explicitly stated as many-to-many (incidents can affect multiple services, services can be affected by multiple incidents), but no constraint prevents the set of affected services from being empty. Should 'one or more' be enforced as a mandatory constraint, or can an incident temporarily have no affected services?

source_references.excerpt: And an incident affects a service?... One or more. Usually one, sometimes several when it's an infrastructure thing.

ambiguities.description: Duplicate relationship asymmetry: The rule states 'an incident is a duplicate of an incident' which is modeled as a self-referential relationship. The acyclic constraint prevents chains, but does this also enforce asymmetry (if B is a duplicate of A, then A is not a duplicate of B)? Or is acyclicity sufficient?

source_references.excerpt: Can a chain form? B duplicates A, C duplicates B?... Everything points at the primary directly... It's wrong. If C duplicates B and B duplicates A, then C should point at A.

ambiguities.description: Manual alert creation by engineers: Lines 25-29 state that engineers can manually create alerts by raising them, which creates an alert record. However, the distinction between automatically generated alerts (from monitoring) and manually created alerts (by engineers) is not modeled. Should there be an Alert subtype or an attribute distinguishing alert source?

source_references.excerpt: An engineer's looking at a dashboard for another reason and spots something... If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.
